Overview and scope
Trevarthen’s theory of primary intersubjectivity treats early mother–infant communication as a coordinated, multimodal “protoconversation” in which facial, prosodic, and gestural signals are synchronized in two-way exchanges that co-create shared affective states. <cite id="e9a1a9d7-0">In this framework, emotions are “a time–space field of intrinsic brain states of mental and behavioral vitality that are signaled for communication to other subjects and that are open to immediate influence from the signals of these others,” and two-way synchronization elicits positive affective effects such as joy and excitement within the interacting dyad</cite>. <cite id="e9a1a9d7-1">Trevarthen emphasizes a two-way traffic of facial, prosodic, and gestural expressions that function as a nonverbal channel for emotion and awareness</cite>, and <cite id="e9a1a9d7-2">his work highlights right-hemisphere responsiveness to maternal prosody and views protoconversation as a right-lateralized, reciprocal, nonverbal emotion-communication system that attunes to and regulates infant autonomic and arousal states</cite>. In broader infant interaction research, “affective intensity” or “arousal” are commonly operationalized through observable behavioral vigor (e.g., intensity of smiling/crying, force or rate of vocalization and facial movements) and physiological indices (e.g., heart rate, heart rate variability, vagal tone), sometimes embedded in state classifications. <cite id="ccb2095b-0">Contemporary accounts also frame “vitality” via timing, pitch, and stress in speech and across modalities, stressing entrainment and “communicative musicality”</cite>. Below, we contrast Trevarthen’s “energetics” with broader “affective intensity/arousal.”

What “energetics” means in Trevarthen’s intersubjective communication
In Trevarthen’s model, “energetics” corresponds to the dynamic vitality of interaction—how exchanges build momentum, tempo, and responsiveness across time—and is enacted primarily through prosody, timing, and multimodal coordination. <cite id="ccb2095b-0">Changes in vitality are enacted through timing, pitch, and stress, and partners often “match and share vitality” across modalities, entering synchronization without exact imitation</cite>. <cite id="e9a1a9d7-0">Two-way traffic of facial, auditory, and tactile emotional signals co-creates a reciprocal system in which joyful pleasure and excitement build within the protoconversation</cite>. <cite id="e9a1a9d7-1">Trevarthen describes a mirror-image two-way exchange of facial, auditory-prosodic, and tactile-gestural signals as the medium for nonverbal emotional communication</cite>, and <cite id="e9a1a9d7-2">notes that infants respond differentially to maternal prosody via the right hemisphere, situating energetic prosodic exchanges within a right-lateralized, reciprocal system</cite>. In parallel, contemporary affect science distinguishes “energetic arousal” from “tense arousal”: <cite id="1c4a5dc3-0">Thayer conceptualizes arousal as comprising energetic arousal (readiness for vigorous, muscular-skeletal activation) and tense arousal (emergency-preparatory activation)</cite>. <cite id="ccb2095b-1">More broadly, hopefulness and grace in movement are framed as qualities of vitality that are sensed by self and other and transmitted relationally</cite>. Together, Trevarthen’s energetics is a relational, bidirectional process—coordinated timing, pitch, and gesture—through which vitality is enacted and mutually regulated in real time.

How infant interaction research typically studies “affective intensity” or “arousal”
In broader infant interaction research, affective intensity or arousal is often operationalized as the magnitude or vigor of behavioral expressions and as indices of autonomic activation. <cite id="1c4a5dc3-1">In dimensional models of emotion, valence and arousal/intensity are core axes, with arousal captured via self-reports, behavioral pacing, or visual/auditory manipulations that increase excitement or calm</cite>. <cite id="1c4a5dc3-2">Physiological markers like skin conductance index arousal, while facial electromyography indexes rapid, partially automatic responses linked to negative affect; self-reported arousal and valence are also used to capture affective intensity</cite>. Developmental work extends this by linking caregiver behavior to infant autonomic regulation: <cite id="e9a1a9d7-2">interpersonal attunement in right-brain–right-brain nonverbal affective communications provides a relational context in which caregivers psychobiologically attune to and regulate infant autonomic and arousal states</cite>. In many paradigms, affective intensity is measured by counts or latencies of smiles/cry/laughter, force or rate of facial muscle activity, acoustic energy in vocalizations, and heart rate or heart-rate variability; these reflect how strongly or intensely an infant or dyad is “activated” at a given moment. <cite id="1c4a5dc3-1">For example, pacing and animation manipulations are used to elicit higher arousal, and physiological or self-report measures capture the resulting intensity</cite>.

Key differences between Trevarthen’s “energetics” and broader affective intensity/arousal
- Level of analysis and directionality:
  - Trevarthen’s energetics emphasizes bidirectional, multimodal resonance and coordination over time; vitality is co-created through synchrony rather than measured as a unidirectional property. <cite id="e9a1a9d7-0">Synchronized two-way traffic of facial, auditory, and tactile signals elicits positive affective effects within the dyad</cite>, and <cite id="ccb2095b-0">partners share and match vitality across modalities through timing and prosodic “communicative musicality”</cite>.
  - Broader infant research often treats affective intensity or arousal as an emergent property of the system or as a state to be inferred from observable vigor and physiological readouts, sometimes from the caregiver or infant alone. <cite id="1c4a5dc3-1">Arousal/intensity is modeled as a dimension and elicited via pacing or visual design, assessed via behavioral and physiological indicators</cite>. <cite id="1c4a5dc3-2">Physiological measures capture arousal intensity during exposure, complemented by self-reports and facial EMG for valence</cite>.
- Emphasis on process vs. magnitude:
  - Trevarthen’s energetics centers on temporal coordination, prosodic pitch/stress, and gesture dynamics—how exchanges gain momentum and then modulate—rather than simply how intense an expression looks or sounds. <cite id="ccb2095b-0">Vitality is enacted through timing, pitch, and stress, and shared by attunement across modalities</cite>. <cite id="e9a1a9d7-0">Excitement builds as the protoconversation proceeds, with immediate interactive effects</cite>.
  - Affective intensity in broader work often emphasizes the magnitude of expression or physiological activation at a point in time (e.g., larger smiles, faster vocal rates, higher heart rate), sometimes framed as arousal level irrespective of coordination quality. <cite id="1c4a5dc3-1">Arousal is treated as intensity ranging from calm to excitement, manipulated by pacing and design</cite>. <cite id="1c4a5dc3-2">Physiological indices (e.g., skin conductance, corrugator EMG) capture intensity or valence-linked arousal</cite>.
- Channels and embodiment:
  - Trevarthen specifies nonverbal channels (face, voice/prosody, touch) as the medium for energizing and regulating interaction; vitality forms span movement “grace” and hopefulness, sensed by self and other. <cite id="e9a1a9d7-1">Visual-facial, auditory-prosodic, and tactile-gestural communications carry emotion and awareness</cite>. <cite id="ccb2095b-1">Adults and infants move in “forms of vitality”; self- and other-sensing of grace and hopefulness in gestural narratives conveys relational feelings</cite>.
  - Broader infant research frequently focuses on specific channels or physiological correlates of intensity (e.g., motor vigor, acoustic energy, heart rate/HRV) as indicators of arousal, sometimes treating these as proxies for affective state without explicit modeling of bidirectional coordination. <cite id="1c4a5dc3-1">Visual and auditory manipulations elicit arousal, with behavioral and self-report measures</cite>. <cite id="1c4a5dc3-2">EMG and skin conductance index arousal and valence; physiological arousal is captured during exposure</cite>.
- Ontology of affect:
  - In Trevarthen’s view, affective states are co-constructed in interaction through resonance and entrainment; “energetics” is how vitality is transmitted and modulated across brains and bodies in real time. <cite id="e9a1a9d7-0">Emotions are fields of brain states of vitality signaled and mutually influenced by others</cite>. <cite id="e9a1a9d7-2">Right-brain-to-right-brain nonverbal affective communications provide a relational context for attunement and regulation of arousal</cite>.
  - In broader work, affective intensity or arousal is often treated as a measurable dimension or state-level property—either experiential (valence–arousal) or physiological—that can be increased or decreased by environmental manipulations; energetic arousal is explicitly distinguished from tense arousal in arousal theory. <cite id="1c4a5dc3-0">Energetic arousal indexes readiness for vigorous activation, while tense arousal indexes emergency-preparatory activation</cite>. <cite id="1c4a5dc3-1">Arousal is commonly operationalized as intensity on behavioral and self-report scales</cite>. <cite id="1c4a5dc3-2">Physiological measures isolate intensity components and valence via facial muscle activity</cite>.

Integrative perspective and bridging concepts
Several bridges clarify how these perspectives align. First, contemporary work explicitly uses “communicative musicality” and “rhythms of dialogue” to capture the energetic coordination Trevarthen emphasizes. <cite id="ccb2095b-0">Scholars highlight synchronization and shared vitality via timing and prosody, replacing purely mind-reading models with embodied, rhythmic attunement</cite>. Second, arousal theory’s “energetic arousal” aligns closely with Trevarthen’s vitality dimension insofar as both concern vigor and readiness for action coordinated between partners. <cite id="1c4a5dc3-0">Energetic arousal is associated with readiness for vigorous, muscular-skeletal activation</cite>, and <cite id="ccb2095b-1">hopefulness and grace in movement are qualities of vitality sensed and shared</cite>. Third, interpersonal neurobiology integrates these views by linking infant protoconversation to regulation of arousal and emotional co-creation. <cite id="e9a1a9d7-2">Right-lateralized, reciprocal nonverbal affective communications serve as a relational context for caregiver–infant attunement to and regulation of infant autonomic and arousal states</cite>. Finally, Stern’s “forms of vitality” articulate a distinct dimension beyond categorical affect, emphasizing that actions reveal feelings of vitality that can be co-experienced and co-regulated in early relationships. <cite id="ccb2095b-2">Vitality forms occupy a dimension apart from affect categories; actions reveal kinematic signatures of social perception, and infants are immersed in the feelings of vitality enacted by caregivers</cite>. In this view, Trevarthen’s energetics is the intersubjective expression and co-regulation of vitality across modalities and time, whereas broader infant research operationalizes affective intensity and arousal as measurable vigor and autonomic activation, sometimes as outcomes elicited by caregiver behaviors or environmental pacing.

Practical implications for measurement and intervention
- Trevarthen-informed measures would prioritize dyadic timing metrics (latency matches, turn-taking regularity), prosodic energy and pitch motion, and multimodal gesture synchrony as indices of energetic coupling, interpreted within episodes that co-create shared affect. <cite id="e9a1a9d7-0">Synchronized two-way traffic elicits positive excitement</cite> and <cite id="ccb2095b-0">partners share vitality across modalities without exact imitation, entering synchronization</cite>.
- Broader infant interaction measures would emphasize behavioral intensity (e.g., number/latency/force of smiles or cries) and physiological arousal (HR/HRV, skin conductance, corrugator EMG) as outcomes, often designed to be increased or decreased by caregiver behaviors. <cite id="1c4a5dc3-1">Pacing and animation manipulate arousal</cite> and <cite id="1c4a5dc3-2">EMG and skin conductance capture valence and arousal intensity during exposure</cite>. Trevarthen’s right-brain prosodic responsiveness can be integrated into these paradigms by manipulating maternal prosody as an energetic cue and monitoring infant right-hemisphere-linked physiological markers. <cite id="e9a1a9d7-2">Infants respond to maternal prosody via the right hemisphere in a right-lateralized, reciprocal system that regulates arousal</cite>.

Summary contrast
- Conceptual locus: Trevarthen’s energetics is a relational, bidirectional process of co-creating and co-regulating vitality through coordinated timing, prosody, and multimodal gesture; broader infant research treats affective intensity and arousal as dimensions or states measured by behavioral vigor and physiological activation. <cite id="e9a1a9d7-0">Emotions are fields of vitality signaled and mutually influenced</cite> and <cite id="ccb2095b-0">vitality is enacted through timing, pitch, and stress via communicative musicality</cite> versus <cite id="1c4a5dc3-1">arousal as intensity from calm to excitement</cite> and <cite id="1c4a5dc3-2">measured via EMG, skin conductance, and self-reports</cite>.
- Mechanisms: Trevarthen emphasizes resonance/entrainment across channels; broader work often emphasizes measurable intensity or autonomic markers per se. <cite id="e9a1a9d7-1">Two-way traffic across face, voice, and touch</cite> and <cite id="ccb2095b-1">gestural forms of vitality</cite> versus <cite id="1c4a5dc3-0">energetic vs. tense arousal</cite> and <cite id="1c4a5dc3-2">physiological arousal indices</cite>.
- Developmental role: Both views agree that caregiver behaviors shape infant arousal and affect; Trevarthen foregrounds intersubjective co-construction, while broader paradigms often operationalize caregiver behavior as an arousal manipulator and infant response as a physiological or behavioral index. <cite id="e9a1a9d7-2">Caregiver attunement regulates infant autonomic and arousal states within a reciprocal nonverbal system</cite> and <cite id="1c4a5dc3-1">manipulations of pacing elicit changes in arousal</cite>.

Caveats and convergence
Trevarthen’s “energetics” is sometimes conflated with “affective intensity,” but they differ in emphasis: energetics is about coupled dynamics and bidirectional regulation of vitality across time and modalities, whereas affective intensity/arousal in broader infant research often indexes moment-to-moment activation magnitude or physiological level. <cite id="ccb2095b-2">Vitality forms are more fundamental than derivative affect categories</cite>, and <cite id="1c4a5dc3-0">energetic arousal aligns with vigor/readiness for action</cite>. Integrative accounts increasingly converge by modeling energetic coordination (timing/pitch/prosody) as causal to changes in arousal and affect, measured via physiological and behavioral indices within dyadic synchrony paradigms. <cite id="ccb2095b-0">Rhythms of dialogue and communicative musicality capture coordinated vitality</cite> and <cite id="e9a1a9d7-2">right-brain prosodic responsiveness situates these energetic exchanges within neural systems that regulate arousal</cite>. </answer>

Title: The Interpersonal Neurobiology of Intersubjectivity
Snippet: Thus, in this protoconversation of synchronized and coordinated visual facial, auditory, and tactile emotional signals, the mother-infant dyad co-creates an intersubjective reciprocal system of nonverbal communication (see Figure 1). Trevarthen concluded that "The emotions constitute a time-space field of intrinsic brain states of mental and behavioral vitality that are signaled for communication to other subjects and that are open to immediate influence from the signals of these others" (Trevarthen, 1993, p. 155). Trevarthen (1990, p. 357) observed that this synchronized two-way traffic of reciprocal nonverbal signals elicits instant emotional effects, namely the positive effects of joyful pleasure and excitement build within the emotion transacting protoconversation. But his synchronization model also focused on internal structure-function events, as he stated "the intrinsic regulators of human brain growth in a child are specifically adapted to be coupled, by emotional communication, to the regulators of adult brains. " These regulated intersubjective interactions permit the intercoordination of positive affective brain states within the emotionally communicating dyad. His work underscored the fundamental principle that the baby's brain is not only affected by these relational emotional transactions, but also its growth literally requires brain-brain interaction in the context of a burgeoning positive affective relationship between the mother and her infant. This fundamental interactive mechanism requires older brains to engage with mental states of awareness, emotion, and interest in younger brains and involves coordination between the subjective feelings of an adult and the intersubjective motivations of the infant to forge an emotional bond with the mother. Trevarthen (1990, p. 335) emphasized the critical role of interpersonal resonance in these intersubjective communications: 

Corresponding generative parameters in…two subjects enable them to resonate with or reflect on one another as minds in expressive bodies. This action pattern can become 'entrained, ' and their experiences can be brought into register and imitated. These are the features that make possible the kind of affectionate empathic communication that occurs, for instance, between young infants and their mothers (1993, p. 126).

Title: The Interpersonal Neurobiology of Intersubjectivity
Snippet: In my own studies on the early development of intersubjective nonverbal emotional communication, I have utilized the interdisciplinary perspectives of interpersonal neurobiology and regulation theory, a theory of the development, psychopathogenesis, and treatment of the subjective self (Schore, 1994(Schore, /2016(Schore, , 2003a(Schore, ,b, 2012a(Schore, , 2019a,b),b). The central focus of this psychoneurobiological model of human development is to more deeply understand the underlying mechanisms by which the structure and function of the mind and brain are shaped by experiences, especially those embedded in emotional relationships, as well as the relational mechanisms by which communicating brains synchronize and align their neural activities with other brains. With respect to this nonverbal communication between brains, I have drawn upon the overlap of Trevarthen's work on intersubjectivity and the Bowlby's on attachment theory. Although the former focused on emotion transacting events early in the 1st year and the latter on emotional events late in the 1st and 2nd year, both offered a similar model of nonverbal visual-facial, auditory-prosodic, and tactile-gestural communications between mother and infant. 

In a mirror image of Trevathen's two-way traffic of emotional facial expressions, gestures, and vocal expressions, Bowlby (1969, p. 120) proposed that mother-infant attachment communications are "accompanied by the strongest of feelings and emotions, and occur within a context of facial expression, posture, and tone of voice. " Interestingly, as opposed to Bowlby, Trevarthen's research was directly informed by extensive studies of developmental brain laterality (see his 1996 "Lateral Asymmetries in Infancy: Implications for the Development of the Hemispheres"). Indeed, in that publication, he noted that the prosody of the voice of the mother is responded to by the infant's right hemisphere.

Title: The Interpersonal Neurobiology of Intersubjectivity
Snippet: Indeed, in that publication, he noted that the prosody of the voice of the mother is responded to by the infant's right hemisphere. He also concluded that "The right hemisphere is more advanced than the left in surface features from about the 25th (gestational) week and this advance persists until the left hemisphere shows a post-natal growth spurt starting in the second year" (Trevarthen, 1996, p. 582). 

Following these valuable leads, in my first book Affect Regulation and the Origin of the Self (1994), I drew upon a large body FIGURE 1 | Channels of face-to-face communication in primary intersubjectivity. Protoconversation is mediated by synchronized intersubjective eye-to-eye orientations, vocalizations, hand gestures, and movements of the arms and head, all acting in coordination to express interpersonal awareness and emotions. From Trevarthen (1993). 

of research on brain laterality and hemispheric asymmetries of structure and function to describe the intersubjective protoconversation as a right-lateralized, reciprocal, and nonverbal emotion communication system. Toward that end, I cited a large number of extant researchers who offered evidence on the early development of right hemisphere (see Schore, 1994Schore, /2016 for references) and concluded that the essential adaptive capacity of intersubjectivity is specifically impacted by the infant's early social experiences. Since these social interactions are occurring in a critical period of right brain growth, the child is using the output of the mother's right cortex as a template for the imprinting, the hard wiring of circuits in his own developing right cortex that will come to mediate his expanding socialemotional capacities to appraise variations in both external and internal information. I further proposed that, over the course of human infancy, these right brain-to-right brain nonverbal affective communications represent a relational context in which the primary caregiver psychobiologically attunes to and regulates the infant's internal states of autonomic nervous system and central nervous system arousal.

Following these valuable leads, in my first book Affect Regulation and the Origin of the Self (1994), I drew upon a large body FIGURE 1 | Channels of face-to-face communication in primary intersubjectivity. Protoconversation is mediated by synchronized intersubjective eye-to-eye orientations, vocalizations, hand gestures, and movements of the arms and head, all acting in coordination to express interpersonal awareness and emotions. From Trevarthen (1993). 

of research on brain laterality and hemispheric asymmetries of structure and function to describe the intersubjective protoconversation as a right-lateralized, reciprocal, and nonverbal emotion communication system. Toward that end, I cited a large number of extant researchers who offered evidence on the early development of right hemisphere (see Schore, 1994Schore, /2016 for references) and concluded that the essential adaptive capacity of intersubjectivity is specifically impacted by the infant's early social experiences. documents.snippet:
Thus, in this protoconversation of synchronized and coordinated visual facial, auditory, and tactile emotional signals, the mother-infant dyad co-creates an intersubjective reciprocal system of nonverbal communication (see Figure 1). Trevarthen concluded that "The emotions constitute a time-space field of intrinsic brain states of mental and behavioral vitality that are signaled for communication to other subjects and that are open to immediate influence from the signals of these others" (Trevarthen, 1993, p. 155). Trevarthen (1990, p. 357) observed that this synchronized two-way traffic of reciprocal nonverbal signals elicits instant emotional effects, namely the positive effects of joyful pleasure and excitement build within the emotion transacting protoconversation. But his synchronization model also focused on internal structure-function events, as he stated "the intrinsic regulators of human brain growth in a child are specifically adapted to be coupled, by emotional communication, to the regulators of adult brains. " These regulated intersubjective interactions permit the intercoordination of positive affective brain states within the emotionally communicating dyad. His work underscored the fundamental principle that the baby's brain is not only affected by these relational emotional transactions, but also its growth literally requires brain-brain interaction in the context of a burgeoning positive affective relationship between the mother and her infant. This fundamental interactive mechanism requires older brains to engage with mental states of awareness, emotion, and interest in younger brains and involves coordination between the subjective feelings of an adult and the intersubjective motivations of the infant to forge an emotional bond with the mother. Trevarthen (1990, p. 335) emphasized the critical role of interpersonal resonance in these intersubjective communications: 

Corresponding generative parameters in…two subjects enable them to resonate with or reflect on one another as minds in expressive bodies. This action pattern can become 'entrained, ' and their experiences can be brought into register and imitated. These are the features that make possible the kind of affectionate empathic communication that occurs, for instance, between young infants and their mothers (1993, p. 126).

documents.title: The Interpersonal Neurobiology of Intersubjectivity
documents.snippet:
In my own studies on the early development of intersubjective nonverbal emotional communication, I have utilized the interdisciplinary perspectives of interpersonal neurobiology and regulation theory, a theory of the development, psychopathogenesis, and treatment of the subjective self (Schore, 1994(Schore, /2016(Schore, , 2003a(Schore, ,b, 2012a(Schore, , 2019a,b),b). The central focus of this psychoneurobiological model of human development is to more deeply understand the underlying mechanisms by which the structure and function of the mind and brain are shaped by experiences, especially those embedded in emotional relationships, as well as the relational mechanisms by which communicating brains synchronize and align their neural activities with other brains. With respect to this nonverbal communication between brains, I have drawn upon the overlap of Trevarthen's work on intersubjectivity and the Bowlby's on attachment theory. Although the former focused on emotion transacting events early in the 1st year and the latter on emotional events late in the 1st and 2nd year, both offered a similar model of nonverbal visual-facial, auditory-prosodic, and tactile-gestural communications between mother and infant. 

In a mirror image of Trevathen's two-way traffic of emotional facial expressions, gestures, and vocal expressions, Bowlby (1969, p. 120) proposed that mother-infant attachment communications are "accompanied by the strongest of feelings and emotions, and occur within a context of facial expression, posture, and tone of voice. " Interestingly, as opposed to Bowlby, Trevarthen's research was directly informed by extensive studies of developmental brain laterality (see his 1996 "Lateral Asymmetries in Infancy: Implications for the Development of the Hemispheres"). Indeed, in that publication, he noted that the prosody of the voice of the mother is responded to by the infant's right hemisphere.

Title: Alert!... Calm Down, There is Nothing to Worry About. Warning and Soothing Speech Synthesis.
Snippet: Dimensional models of emotion attempt to conceptualize human emotions by their position in two or three dimensional space. Practically all of them incorporate valence and arousal or intensity dimensions. 

Thayer distinguishes two dimensions of subjective arousal; energetic arousal (EA) and tense arousal (TA). Energetic arousal is associated with readiness for vigorous and muscular-skeletal activation. Tense arousal represents a preparatory-emergency system, activated by some real or imagined danger. (Thayer 1989) We think that the notions of "tense arousal" and "emergency-preparatory activation" best describe the affective phenomenon which influence on speech we want to study.

Title: The Chart Excites Me! Exploring How Data Visualization Design Influences Affective Arousal
Snippet: Affective arousal is about the activation of emotion [4] and is viewed as a key construct of human affects. For example, the well-known circumplex model [4] views affects as combinations of valence and arousal. While valence describes whether an affect is positive or negative, arousal reflects the intensity of the affect, ranging from calm to excitement. Along with the conceptualization of affective arousal, many researchers began to conduct studies to investigate how to elicit affective arousal specifically. For example, Sundar and Kalyanaraman [27] examined the relationship between animation and affective arousal using physiological indicators. Lang et al. [28] and Gorn et al. [29] used self-report methods to gather ratings from users and assess how color and pacing influenced perceived arousal. 

Meanwhile, as affective arousal is closely related to people's reactions, behaviors, and information processing [8], it has been massively studied in research about visual communication, such as web advertising and TV broadcasting. For example, Singh and Hitchon [30] reviewed dozens of studies conducted in the last century that examined arousal-centered topics, such as how to arouse viewers most advantageously in a TV show and how to increase consumers' desire for a product by eliciting arousal. Given the fundamental role of affective arousal, this thread of research continues to prosper until today while dealing with trending topics such as how to design arousing games, user interfaces, or immersive environments [27], [31], [32]. For example, Aoki et al. [33] examined how to design chat balloons that represent various levels of arousal in text chats. Cusveller et al. [32] explored how to evoke affective arousal in computer games. 

This work follows this research thread and studies affective arousal specifically in the context of visualization design. We see this work as an initial step towards exploring what design factors contribute to affective arousal in data visualization.

Title: Replicating and Extending Soroka, Fournier, and Nir: Negative News Increases Arousal and Negative Affect
Snippet: SFN theorised and tested the effect of negative news on arousal.Yet, theories in psychology and neuroscience on the structure of affect indicate that affect consists of (at least) two dimensions.Arousal captures the intensity of the affective experience, but this intensity can be both negative and positive.Valence is the second dimension of affect and captures the directionality of the affect, ranging from positive to negative (Schiller et al., 2022).SCLs-which SFN used-capture arousal but do not distinguish the valence of the affective experience (Dawson et al., 2007).To capture valence, we turned to facial electromyography (fEMG) which registers rapid, partially automatic affective responses in the face while participants view stimulus material.fEMG is primarily used as an indicator of emotional valence (Larsen et al., 2003).We focus on the corrugator supercilii muscle region which is the muscle above the eyebrow that draws the brow down and pulls the brows together.The corrugator is used as an indicator of negative affect, also in political communication research.For instance, in response to political communication, messages incongruent with held beliefs produced more corrugator activity (negative affect) than congruent communication (Bakker, Schumacher, & Rooduijn, 2021;Boyer, 2023).We extend SFN and preregistered that we expect that negative news compared to positive news increases the activity of the corrugator muscle (H2).

Second, we broaden SFN by also measuring self-reported valence and arousal.SFN did not collect measures of either but did ask about the "tone of the message" which was: "Please rank this story on the following dimensions….Negativity."That is, however, not the same as measuring the affective response to the message.We agree with SFN that physiological measures have the advantage that they capture affective responses during exposure.

Title: On the dynamics of Zoom fatigue
Snippet: In everyday speech, changes in vitality enacted through timing, pitch and stress procures the experience of talking to an actual, living person (as opposed to the flat and monotonous intonation of robots in old sci-fi movies). Furthermore, during everyday interaction, we often match and share vitality across sense modalities, or what is also known as affect attunement: We express the vitality of another person's actions without imitating their exact behavioral expression. By doing so, we are effectively brought into synchronization with each other. At this basic level of intercorporeality, no mind reading is needed. Building on these insights, scholars have therefore begun to replace the ocularcentric metaphor of mind reading with more embodied metaphors like rhythms of dialogue (Jaffe et al., 2001) and communicative musicality (Malloch and Trevarthen, 2009). Instead of cognitive 'in-sight', these metaphors stress the fundamental importance of coordinating bodily movements over time, of getting 'in-tune' and 'in-sync' with each other.

Title: The Human Nature of Music
Snippet: As Daniel Stern has written (Stern, 2010), the human body has a rich range of gestural 'forms of vitality' -we move in musical ways. And within each actor there is both 'self-sensing' and 'other-sensing' of the degree of grace, or biological efficiency (Bernstein, 1967) and hopefulness (Trevarthen and Malloch, 2017a) in the gestural narratives of our projects. These qualities of vitality, or well-being, transmitted to others, become the qualities of relationships and social activities -their moral values (Kirschner and Tomasello, 2010;Narvaez, 2014;Trainor and Cirelli, 2015). They convey relational feelings for the degree of consensuality or sharing of expression in moving. Effort to manage the grace and morality of movements can be cultivated to assist well-being of those whose actions are confused or fearful -that is, the making or 'poetry' (from the Greek poiein, to make) of their movements may be enhanced to provide responsive and relational care or therapy (Hobson, 1985, ch3;Stern, 2000, p. xiv;Osborne, 2009b;Meares, 2016). 

At times our healthy ability for graceful gesturing is met with circumstances that do not allow it to be expressed with its natural healthy vitality. For example, failure to gain a sympathetic appreciation of their musicality can cause an infant to express withdrawal and distress (Murray and Trevarthen, 1985). Instead of joyful pride in sharing play they show sadness and shame (Trevarthen, 2005b). However, an infant's communicative musicality can also be expressive of resilience and determination. 

In the example presented in Figure 5A we see a consistent rigidity of expression and a lack of self-confident invention on the part of a mother suffering from BPD (borderline personality disorder). She repeats the same up-and-down vocal gesture again and again, with almost no vocal participation on the part of the infant.

Title: A glimpse into social perception in light of vitality forms
Snippet: In Stern's approach, social perception activities take parental-infant dyadic relationships as proto-types. Vitality forms occupy a new dimension apart from affective category theory, actions per se convey enough in revealing the kinematic signatures of social perception. To adults, previous parentalinfant intersubjective activities may remain components in the adult stage. Vitality forms should be seen as more fundamental than derivative categories of affects, and contents or intentions of mindreading. Thus, more or less metaphorically, not only infants but also adults are immersed in "feelings of vitality": "Different feelings of vitality can be expressed in a multitude of parental acts that do not qualify as "regular" affective acts: how the mother picks up baby, folds the diapers, grooms her hair or the baby's hair, reaches for a bottle, unbuttons her blouse. The infant is immersed in these "feelings of vitality"" (Stern, 1998, p. 54). 

Another important person in the realm of developmental intersubjectivity studies, Trevarthen (2013) applauds highly of Stern's last monograph on forms of vitality, "has made a bible for all humanistic and art therapies" (Trevarthen, 2013, p. 44). In a sense, vitality forms play a constitutive role in the bottom level of the stratified structures of intersubjectivity. Combining Trevarthen's concept of primary intersubjectivity (the stage of young infants before 9 months), vitality forms are the first perceivable signatures that young infants can see (directly) (cf. Gallagher, 2020). However, it is far from clear "how body, brain, and mind collaborate in its shared vitality" (Trevarthen, 2019, p. 31) based on the current empirical studies of vitality forms. 

Further, in this article, possible types of vitality forms related to other minds are collected and discussed in the following four areas across two dimensions of criteria, which have been brought to particular attention in recent years:

Furthermore, during everyday interaction, we often match and share vitality across sense modalities, or what is also known as affect attunement: We express the vitality of another person's actions without imitating their exact behavioral expression. By doing so, we are effectively brought into synchronization with each other. At this basic level of intercorporeality, no mind reading is needed. Building on these insights, scholars have therefore begun to replace the ocularcentric metaphor of mind reading with more embodied metaphors like rhythms of dialogue (Jaffe et al., 2001) and communicative musicality (Malloch and Trevarthen, 2009). Instead of cognitive 'in-sight', these metaphors stress the fundamental importance of coordinating bodily movements over time, of getting 'in-tune' and 'in-sync' with each other.

documents.title: The Human Nature of Music
documents.snippet:
As Daniel Stern has written (Stern, 2010), the human body has a rich range of gestural 'forms of vitality' -we move in musical ways. And within each actor there is both 'self-sensing' and 'other-sensing' of the degree of grace, or biological efficiency (Bernstein, 1967) and hopefulness (Trevarthen and Malloch, 2017a) in the gestural narratives of our projects. These qualities of vitality, or well-being, transmitted to others, become the qualities of relationships and social activities -their moral values (Kirschner and Tomasello, 2010;Narvaez, 2014;Trainor and Cirelli, 2015). They convey relational feelings for the degree of consensuality or sharing of expression in moving. Effort to manage the grace and morality of movements can be cultivated to assist well-being of those whose actions are confused or fearful -that is, the making or 'poetry' (from the Greek poiein, to make) of their movements may be enhanced to provide responsive and relational care or therapy (Hobson, 1985, ch3;Stern, 2000, p. xiv;Osborne, 2009b;Meares, 2016). 

At times our healthy ability for graceful gesturing is met with circumstances that do not allow it to be expressed with its natural healthy vitality. For example, failure to gain a sympathetic appreciation of their musicality can cause an infant to express withdrawal and distress (Murray and Trevarthen, 1985). Instead of joyful pride in sharing play they show sadness and shame (Trevarthen, 2005b). However, an infant's communicative musicality can also be expressive of resilience and determination. 

In the example presented in Figure 5A we see a consistent rigidity of expression and a lack of self-confident invention on the part of a mother suffering from BPD (borderline personality disorder). She repeats the same up-and-down vocal gesture again and again, with almost no vocal participation on the part of the infant.

documents.title: A glimpse into social perception in light of vitality forms
documents.snippet:
In Stern's approach, social perception activities take parental-infant dyadic relationships as proto-types. Vitality forms occupy a new dimension apart from affective category theory, actions per se convey enough in revealing the kinematic signatures of social perception. To adults, previous parentalinfant intersubjective activities may remain components in the adult stage. Vitality forms should be seen as more fundamental than derivative categories of affects, and contents or intentions of mindreading. Thus, more or less metaphorically, not only infants but also adults are immersed in "feelings of vitality": "Different feelings of vitality can be expressed in a multitude of parental acts that do not qualify as "regular" affective acts: how the mother picks up baby, folds the diapers, grooms her hair or the baby's hair, reaches for a bottle, unbuttons her blouse. The infant is immersed in these "feelings of vitality"" (Stern, 1998, p. 54). 

Another important person in the realm of developmental intersubjectivity studies, Trevarthen (2013) applauds highly of Stern's last monograph on forms of vitality, "has made a bible for all humanistic and art therapies" (Trevarthen, 2013, p. 44). In a sense, vitality forms play a constitutive role in the bottom level of the stratified structures of intersubjectivity. Combining Trevarthen's concept of primary intersubjectivity (the stage of young infants before 9 months), vitality forms are the first perceivable signatures that young infants can see (directly) (cf. Gallagher, 2020). However, it is far from clear "how body, brain, and mind collaborate in its shared vitality" (Trevarthen, 2019, p. 31) based on the current empirical studies of vitality forms.

attempts.answer:
Overview and definitions

In Trevarthen’s framework, communication is multimodal and temporally organized across three interlocking dimensions: kinematics (the temporal patterning of movements), physiognomics (configurations of body, posture, gesture, face, and voice that set the scene of action and expression), and energetics (variations in intensity, force, and vigor that modulate action and sound). <cite id="89102b51-1">Imitative intersubjective encounters reveal coordination within- and between-subjects across three essential dimensions of communication—kinematics (temporal patterns of movements), physiognomics (shape of body and organizing postural, gestural, facial or vocal settings tied to interest and purpose), and energetics (intensity, force, or power of actions)</cite>. These dimensions do not operate as separate channels but as components of a coordinative structure that can regulate mutual attention and transfer mental activity between participants. <cite id="89102b51-1">According to Trevarthen’s Theory of Innate Intersubjectivity, imitation dynamically regulates transfer of motives and emotions between minds, coordinating these three dimensions to motivate learning in human communities</cite>. <cite id="89102b51-2">Trevarthen’s account situates this coordination within face-to-face, right-brain–linked nonverbal systems supporting mutual play and mutual love, with hyperscanning evidence indicating a co-constructed, nonverbal emotional communication system</cite>.

Why coordination across all three is necessary for intersubjectivity

Intersubjectivity requires that participants jointly regulate attention, share a common ground of intention, and build mutual coherence in emotion and meaning. <cite id="89102b51-1">Trevarthen argues that coordination across kinematics, physiognomics, and energetics is how imitation transfers motives and emotions between minds, yielding a dynamic intersubjective regulatory function</cite>. <cite id="35f15c40-2">In Trevarthen and Aitken’s formulation, intersubjectivity is manifested when a mother and baby mutually respond to each other’s emotions, building mutual coherence that underpins attachment</cite>. Each dimension contributes a distinct but interdependent layer: kinematics supplies the temporal coupling that aligns actions and responses; physiognomics provides categorical settings and iconic mapping that link forms to states of mind; and energetics modulates emphasis, urgency, or calm that indexes affective valence and commitment. <cite id="89102b51-1">Physiognomics organizes postural, gestural, facial, and vocal settings into categories aligned with the actor’s changing interests and purposes, while energetics varies intensity and force; together, these specify a shared “scene” and action plan that can be noticed, predicted, and co-constructed</cite>.

Crucially, when these dimensions are co-ordinated—timing, form, and intensity co-vary in moment-to-moment synchrony—participants can infer shared attention and intention, not merely reactive stimulus–response. <cite id="ad01463b-0">Prosodic structure and bodily movement are tightly intertwined: pitch accents and boundary tones anchor prominent phases in body movement; prosody and gesture jointly highlight and disambiguate linguistic structure and convey speaker emotion, beliefs, and attitudes</cite>. <cite id="ad01463b-1">Fine-grained alignment between prosodic contours, intensity shifts, and facial/gestural cues (eyebrow movement, eye blinks, mouth shape) enhances emotional clarity, communicative precision, and recognition of mental states, supporting rapport and empathy</cite>. <cite id="ad01463b-2">Gesture’s hierarchical phrasing and prominence align with prosodic prominence and phrasal grouping, with large gestures matching more prosodically prominent syllables; prosody thus coordinates spoken and gestural elements as a unified, modality‑independent structure</cite>. Trevarthen’s kinematics–physiognomics–energetics scheme captures exactly these multimodal couplings at the microstructure of interaction (temporal phase, embodied category, and energetic emphasis), so their joint coordination creates a shared “frame” for action and meaning that goes beyond parallel but unshared signals.

From interaction to intersubjectivity: the missing link is shared intentionality

Interaction can involve coordinated movements or facial mimicry without shared intention; intersubjectivity emerges when kinematic timing, physiognomic category mapping, and energetic emphasis mutually index the same goal or state and are co-regulated in real time. <cite id="89102b51-1">Imitative encounters that coordinate the three dimensions regulate processes in which motives and emotions are transferred between minds, with correspondence defined by timing, form, and intensity rather than static form alone</cite>. <cite id="89102b51-1">Trevarthen contrasts this with accounts that treat correspondence as purely static or one-person-view, emphasizing that true intersubjectivity is face-to-face, two-way communication where co-ordinated timing, form, and intensity signal alignment of interest and purpose</cite>. If only one or two dimensions operate in a fragmented way—say, kinematic synchrony without matching physiognomic category settings or energetic modulation—the participants remain behaviorally coupled but lack a shared “scene” of action and feeling; the relation degrades to stimulus–response mimicry rather than mutual regulation of a common goal. <cite id="ad01463b-1">Only when prosody, facial expressions, and gestures are tightly aligned do listeners gain access to social intent and emotional nuance, enabling empathy and rapport; treating modalities independently erodes communicative precision</cite>. Trevarthen’s framework thus treats the three dimensions as jointly necessary because they provide the multimodal “currency” for shared intention: timing aligns agendas, form maps meanings, and energy signals engagement, together constituting a coordinative structure for protoconversations.

Developmental grounding: from protoconversations to shared meaning

Trevarthen’s program is explicitly developmental: early parent–infant exchanges build primary intersubjectivity by co-ordinating these dimensions in small, protodeclarative acts that establish joint attention and mutual regulation. <cite id="89102b51-1">Imitative encounters organize learning in human communities and transfer motives and emotions between minds, with kinematics, physiognomics, and energetics changing as infants’ motives and purposes develop</cite>. <cite id="35f15c40-2">Mutual emotional responsiveness builds mutual coherence, leading to secure attachment</cite>. Contemporary work on body rhythms and haptic/kinesthetic coupling extends this, showing interpersonal resonance mechanisms that underwrite primary intersubjectivity and suggest how kinematic phase-locking with energetic and facial modulation supports shared affect and intention. <cite id="89102b51-0">Micro-rhythms and phase relations in bodily contact reveal mechanisms of interpersonal resonance, contributing to understanding primary intersubjectivity, embodied affectivity, and affective intention with prototypes in early infant–caregiver interaction</cite>. In other words, the three dimensions do not just describe behavior; they specify the multimodal scaffolding by which protoconversational agents align agendas, map actions to meanings, and regulate each other’s states—operations that are the essence of intersubjectivity and fail if any dimension is absent or out-of-step.

Neurophenomenological support and the intersubjective channel

Trevarthen’s account has been linked to right-brain, multimodal systems for nonverbal social cognition, consistent with the view that coordinated kinematics–physiognomics–energetics ride on a dedicated intersubjective channel. <cite id="89102b51-2">Right temporoparietal junction and right-brain networks support face-to-face nonverbal communication; developmentally, right-brain intersubjectivity underpins mutual play and mutual love, with hyperscanning showing a co-constructed, nonverbal emotional communication system</cite>. Such neurocognitive architecture favors integrated prosody–gesture–face coordination over isolated channels; it explains why isolating one dimension (e.g., kinematic movement without facial/energetic modulation) yields at best mimicry, not shared meaning. <cite id="ad01463b-0">Prosody and gesture co-occur temporally and jointly influence semantic/pragmatic processing and emotion, suggesting that separating them degrades both informational and affective content</cite>.

Putting it together: why all three must operate together

- Mechanistically: kinematics supplies temporal phase-locking; physiognomics provides categorical mapping of state and action; energetics signals engagement and valence. <cite id="89102b51-1">Coordinating these three dimensions in imitation dynamically regulates the transfer of motives and emotions between minds</cite>. 
- Phenomenally: this multimodal alignment yields clarity of social intent, emotional nuance, and mutual coherence—hallmarks of intersubjectivity—rather than reflexive interaction. <cite id="ad01463b-1">Alignment across prosody, facial expressions, and gestures enhances communicative precision and recognition of mental states, supporting empathy and rapport</cite>. 
- Developmentally: these co-ordinated couplings scaffold protoconversations and attachment, with their absence or misalignment leaving only stimulus–response coupling. <cite id="35f15c40-2">Mutual coherence in emotional responsiveness builds attachment</cite>. 
- Neurocognitively: right-brain networks and hyperscanning evidence support a co-constructed, multimodal nonverbal system that integrates timing, form, and intensity. <cite id="89102b51-2">A right-brain-to-right-brain nonverbal emotional communication system underlies co-constructed relationships</cite>.

Therefore, Trevarthen’s framework requires all three dimensions to operate in coordinated synchrony because their integrated co-variation creates a multimodal coordinative structure—shared timing, category mapping, and energetic emphasis—that mutually regulates attention and intention, producing intersubjective understanding. When any dimension is missing or poorly coordinated, participants remain behaviorally interactive but lack the mutual coherence and shared meaning that define intersubjectivity. <cite id="89102b51-1">Coordinated kinematics, physiognomics, and energetics regulate transfer of motives and emotions and organize learning in communities</cite> <cite id="ad01463b-0">Prosody and gesture are tightly intertwined temporally and pragmatically, jointly conveying emphasis, emotion, and referential clarity</cite> <cite id="ad01463b-1">Fine-grained multimodal alignment enhances communicative precision and social intent understanding</cite> <cite id="35f15c40-2">Intersubjectivity emerges from mutual coherence in emotional responsiveness</cite> <cite id="89102b51-2">A co-constructed, nonverbal right-brain system supports this intersubjective coordination</cite>.

Title: Exploring Spontaneous Imitation in Infancy: A Three Generation Inter-Familial Study
Snippet: This study has been carried out within the frame of the Theory of Innate Intersubjectivity (Trevarthen, 1993), according to which imitation has a dynamic intersubjective regulatory function. Imitation constitutes the process in which mental activity-including motives and emotions-is transferred between minds but the message it conveys changes according to age-related developments of infant's motives (Trevarthen, Kokkinaki, & Fiamenghi, 1999). 

Imitative intersubjective encounters with infants reveal coordination within-and between-subjects in three essential dimensions of communication that motivate learning in a human community: "kinematics" (the temporal patterns of movements), "physiognomics" (changes in the shape of the body, organizing postural, gestural, facial or vocal settings in distinct categories related to the subject's changing interest and purposes) and "energetics" (variations in the intensity, force or power of actions) (Trevarthen, 1986). 

Both Meltzoff and Trevarthen attempt to conceptualize the origins of a theory of mind in infancy. For each, mind begins with a shared mind, a highly pre-symbolic representational intelligence and the central question is, for both, how can an infant sense the state of the other? Both theories posit that the motivated and intentional infant's perception of correspondence is the central mechanism in the creation of intersubjectivity (Beebe, Sorter, Rustin, & Knoblauch, 2003). Two points of difference stand out: the definition of correspondence/matching and the theory of mind underlying infant intersubjectivity. Regarding the first point of difference, for Meltzoff, the definition of correspondence rests on form, while for Trevarthen, correspondence is defined by behavioral similarities in timing, form and intensity. Despite the fact that Meltzoff acknowledges the importance of parent-infant imitation games, he studies the behavior of infants within an experiment, one-person view, and his concept of correspondence is more static than Trevarthen's who studies face-to-face two way communication.

Substantivflexion soll die explanative Adaquatheit und Pradiktabilitat des Konzepts hinsichtlich des Aufbaus und der Veranderung eines Teilflexionssystems als Ganzes uberpruft und auf dieser Basis ein Strukturmodell der dt. Substantivflexion vorgeschlagen werden. Insbesondere bei der Erfassung der Gesamtstruktur des Teilflexionssystems werden dabei Probleme des zugrundegelegten theoretischen Ansatzes deutlich werden. Mit der Diskussion und der Uberprufung theoretischer Annahmen, die diese Probleme losen konnen, sowie der detaillierten Analyse des Flexionsverhaltens der dt. Substantive soll ein Beitrag zur weiteren Ausformulierung des in eine allgemeine Praferenztheorie einzuordnenden theoretischen Konzepts der Naturlichen Morphologie wie auch zur germanistischen Forschung geleistet werden.
</snippet>

Title: Exploring Spontaneous Imitation in Infancy: A Three Generation Inter-Familial Study
Snippet: This study has been carried out within the frame of the Theory of Innate Intersubjectivity (Trevarthen, 1993), according to which imitation has a dynamic intersubjective regulatory function. Imitation constitutes the process in which mental activity-including motives and emotions-is transferred between minds but the message it conveys changes according to age-related developments of infant's motives (Trevarthen, Kokkinaki, & Fiamenghi, 1999). 

Imitative intersubjective encounters with infants reveal coordination within-and between-subjects in three essential dimensions of communication that motivate learning in a human community: "kinematics" (the temporal patterns of movements), "physiognomics" (changes in the shape of the body, organizing postural, gestural, facial or vocal settings in distinct categories related to the subject's changing interest and purposes) and "energetics" (variations in the intensity, force or power of actions) (Trevarthen, 1986). 

Both Meltzoff and Trevarthen attempt to conceptualize the origins of a theory of mind in infancy. For each, mind begins with a shared mind, a highly pre-symbolic representational intelligence and the central question is, for both, how can an infant sense the state of the other? Both theories posit that the motivated and intentional infant's perception of correspondence is the central mechanism in the creation of intersubjectivity (Beebe, Sorter, Rustin, & Knoblauch, 2003). Two points of difference stand out: the definition of correspondence/matching and the theory of mind underlying infant intersubjectivity. Regarding the first point of difference, for Meltzoff, the definition of correspondence rests on form, while for Trevarthen, correspondence is defined by behavioral similarities in timing, form and intensity. Despite the fact that Meltzoff acknowledges the importance of parent-infant imitation games, he studies the behavior of infants within an experiment, one-person view, and his concept of correspondence is more static than Trevarthen's who studies face-to-face two way communication.
</snippet>

Title: Prosody in the Auditory and Visual Domains: A Developmental Perspective
Snippet: The speech and gesture dimensions of prosody are found to be tightly intertwined at the temporal, semantic, and pragmatic levels, and this is true not only in adult speech but also in language development. 

Speakers' body movements are temporally coordinated with the prosodic structure in speech, pitch accents and boundary tones serving as anchoring points for prominent phases in body movements (Hadar et al., 1983;De Ruiter, 1998;Leonard and Cummins, 2011;Esteve-Gibert and Prieto, 2013;Ishi et al., 2014;Ambrazaitis and House, 2017;Esteve-Gibert et al., 2017a). At the semantic and pragmatic levels, prosody and gestures can both have a deictic component through which speakers highlight certain elements in speech (Levelt et al., 1985;Roustan and Dohen, 2010), they can disambiguate syntactic constituents (Guellaï et al., 2014;Krivokapic et al., 2016), and mutually influence the processing of speaker's emotions, beliefs, and attitudes (Ekman, 1979;Kendon, 2004;Poggi et al., 2013). In the multimodal expression of prosody, the gesture dimension can consist of movements of the hand or head, facial expressions, or body postures. Traditionally, different types of body movements have been studied independently (for instance, facial expressions have received more attention in the literature on emotions, while hand movements have been the focus of studies on the referential value of gestures in language). In the present paper we will refer to these different types of movements as 'gestures, ' as we propose that it is more interesting to take them as a whole to have a complete picture of the speech-gesture relationship in language and communication development.
</snippet>

Title: Multimodal Emotion Coupling via Speech-to-Facial and Bodily Gestures in Dyadic Interaction
Snippet: Human communication is inherently multimodal, relying on the tightly coordinated interplay of speech, facial expressions, and gestures to convey not just linguistic content but emotional nuance and social intent. This phenomenon, referred to as multimodal synchronization, supports not only information transmission but also interpersonal rapport, empathy, and emotional resonance [1,2,3]. It is this fine-grained, moment-to-moment alignment across modalities that defines naturalistic emotional communication-and understanding its structure remains a central challenge in affective computing [4,5]. 

One well-studied form of multimodal synchrony is the coupling of speech prosody with facial expressions. Temporal alignment between pitch contours, intensity shifts, and speech rhythm with facial gestures-such as eyebrow movements, eye blinks, and mouth shape-enhances emotional clarity, communicative precision, and improves the recognition of emotional states and facilitates deeper interpersonal connection [1,2,6,7]. It plays a particularly important role in emotionally salient contexts, such as disagreement, persuasion, or empathy. Despite its centrality in human interaction, computational systems for emotion recognition have often treated these modalities independently, applying either coarse-grained averaging or ignoring their temporal dependencies altogether [8]. 

In parallel, hand and upper-body gestures-although long recognized as integral to co-speech communication-remain underrepresented in computational models of emotional synchrony. Gestures serve a range of communicative and affective functions: they can emphasize speech, mirror prosodic structure, reveal internal emotional states, and provide a channel for self-regulation. Co-speech gestures have been shown to temporally align with prosodic and semantic features of speech, enhancing the expressiveness, rhythm, and emotional clarity of interaction [9,10,11,12]. When coordinated with vocal and facial signals, gestures contribute to a more embodied and behaviorally grounded portrayal of affect. This coordination has particular significance in neurodiverse and developmentally diverse populations, where gesture may amplify or compensate for less expressive verbal or facial signals [13,14].
</snippet>

Title: Multidimensional Labeling of Gesture in Communication: the M3D Proposal
Snippet: It has long been attested that spoken prosody and gesture are closely linked-not only do their prominent parts generally co-occur in time, but recent studies show they may also be connected in space, with larger gestures matching more prosodically prominent syllables (Ambrazaitis & House, 2023). This close link between movement and speech even serves as the basis for the Articulatory Phonology framework, whereby gestures of the mouth (including lip and tongue movements) correlate with auditory prosodic modulations (Parrell et al., 2014;Krivokapic et al., 2017). The M3D proposal aligns with the conceptualization of prosody as articulated by Prieto, Esteve-Gibert, and Shattuck-Hufnagel (2025), which posits that prosody operates as a unified, modality-independent structure, coordinating both spoken and gestural elements of communication. 

Prosodic structure has been described more abstractly as the raw organizational structure within which an utterance is hierarchically organized into phonologically defined constituents with heads (Beckman, 1996, p. 19). Two main aspects of prosody (that is, prominence and phrasal grouping) can be expressed through bodily visual means as well as through acoustic cues in speech. In fact, Kendon's (1980) description of the hierarchical organization of gesture movements parallel the hierarchical structure of speech prosody, where large gesture units can be broken down into one or a series of gesture phrases (i.e., individual gestures), which in turn can be divided into even smaller gesture phases (i.e., different stages in the execution of a gesture), with stroke phases being the only obligatory and most prominent phase. 

Following this line of research, M3D proposes a system to assess how visual bodily properties are temporally organized and relate to the prosodic dimension of language by specifically annotating two main aspects of gesture, namely gestural movement organization into constituents (i.e., phasing and phrasing properties), as well as their prominence properties. Importantly, these prosodic characteristics refer specifically to gesture and not to acoustic prosody.
</snippet></tool_output><think>

Overview and definitions

In Trevarthen’s framework, communication is multimodal and temporally organized across three interlocking dimensions: kinematics (the temporal patterning of movements), physiognomics (configurations of body, posture, gesture, face, and voice that set the scene of action and expression), and energetics (variations in intensity, force, and vigor that modulate action and sound). <cite id="89102b51-1">Imitative intersubjective encounters reveal coordination within- and between-subjects across three essential dimensions of communication—kinematics (temporal patterns of movements), physiognomics (shape of body and organizing postural, gestural, facial or vocal settings tied to interest and purpose), and energetics (intensity, force, or power of actions)</cite>. These dimensions do not operate as separate channels but as components of a coordinative structure that can regulate mutual attention and transfer mental activity between participants. <cite id="89102b51-1">According to Trevarthen’s Theory of Innate Intersubjectivity, imitation dynamically regulates transfer of motives and emotions between minds, coordinating these three dimensions to motivate learning in human communities</cite>. <cite id="89102b51-2">Trevarthen’s account situates this coordination within face-to-face, right-brain–linked nonverbal systems supporting mutual play and mutual love, with hyperscanning evidence indicating a co-constructed, nonverbal emotional communication system</cite>.

Why coordination across all three is necessary for intersubjectivity

Intersubjectivity requires that participants jointly regulate attention, share a common ground of intention, and build mutual coherence in emotion and meaning. <cite id="89102b51-1">Trevarthen argues that coordination across kinematics, physiognomics, and energetics is how imitation transfers motives and emotions between minds, yielding a dynamic intersubjective regulatory function</cite>. <cite id="35f15c40-2">In Trevarthen and Aitken’s formulation, intersubjectivity is manifested when a mother and baby mutually respond to each other’s emotions, building mutual coherence that underpins attachment</cite>. Each dimension contributes a distinct but interdependent layer: kinematics supplies the temporal coupling that aligns actions and responses; physiognomics provides categorical settings and iconic mapping that link forms to states of mind; and energetics modulates emphasis, urgency, or calm that indexes affective valence and commitment. <cite id="89102b51-1">Physiognomics organizes postural, gestural, facial, and vocal settings into categories aligned with the actor’s changing interests and purposes, while energetics varies intensity and force; together, these specify a shared “scene” and action plan that can be noticed, predicted, and co-constructed</cite>.

Crucially, when these dimensions are co-ordinated—timing, form, and intensity co-vary in moment-to-moment synchrony—participants can infer shared attention and intention, not merely reactive stimulus–response. <cite id="ad01463b-0">Prosodic structure and bodily movement are tightly intertwined: pitch accents and boundary tones anchor prominent phases in body movement; prosody and gesture jointly highlight and disambiguate linguistic structure and convey speaker emotion, beliefs, and attitudes</cite>. <cite id="ad01463b-1">Fine-grained alignment between prosodic contours, intensity shifts, and facial/gestural cues (eyebrow movement, eye blinks, mouth shape) enhances emotional clarity, communicative precision, and recognition of mental states, supporting rapport and empathy</cite>. <cite id="ad01463b-2">Gesture’s hierarchical phrasing and prominence align with prosodic prominence and phrasal grouping, with large gestures matching more prosodically prominent syllables; prosody thus coordinates spoken and gestural elements as a unified, modality‑independent structure</cite>. Trevarthen’s kinematics–physiognomics–energetics scheme captures exactly these multimodal couplings at the microstructure of interaction (temporal phase, embodied category, and energetic emphasis), so their joint coordination creates a shared “frame” for action and meaning that goes beyond parallel but unshared signals.

From interaction to intersubjectivity: the missing link is shared intentionality

Interaction can involve coordinated movements or facial mimicry without shared intention; intersubjectivity emerges when kinematic timing, physiognomic category mapping, and energetic emphasis mutually index the same goal or state and are co-regulated in real time. <cite id="89102b51-1">Imitative encounters that coordinate the three dimensions regulate processes in which motives and emotions are transferred between minds, with correspondence defined by timing, form, and intensity rather than static form alone</cite>. <cite id="89102b51-1">Trevarthen contrasts this with accounts that treat correspondence as purely static or one-person-view, emphasizing that true intersubjectivity is face-to-face, two-way communication where co-ordinated timing, form, and intensity signal alignment of interest and purpose</cite>. If only one or two dimensions operate in a fragmented way—say, kinematic synchrony without matching physiognomic category settings or energetic modulation—the participants remain behaviorally coupled but lack a shared “scene” of action and feeling; the relation degrades to stimulus–response mimicry rather than mutual regulation of a common goal. <cite id="ad01463b-1">Only when prosody, facial expressions, and gestures are tightly aligned do listeners gain access to social intent and emotional nuance, enabling empathy and rapport; treating modalities independently erodes communicative precision</cite>. Trevarthen’s framework thus treats the three dimensions as jointly necessary because they provide the multimodal “currency” for shared intention: timing aligns agendas, form maps meanings, and energy signals engagement, together constituting a coordinative structure for protoconversations.

Developmental grounding: from protoconversations to shared meaning

Trevarthen’s program is explicitly developmental: early parent–infant exchanges build primary intersubjectivity by co-ordinating these dimensions in small, protodeclarative acts that establish joint attention and mutual regulation. <cite id="89102b51-1">Imitative encounters organize learning in human communities and transfer motives and emotions between minds, with kinematics, physiognomics, and energetics changing as infants’ motives and purposes develop</cite>. <cite id="35f15c40-2">Mutual emotional responsiveness builds mutual coherence, leading to secure attachment</cite>. Contemporary work on body rhythms and haptic/kinesthetic coupling extends this, showing interpersonal resonance mechanisms that underwrite primary intersubjectivity and suggest how kinematic phase-locking with energetic and facial modulation supports shared affect and intention. <cite id="89102b51-0">Micro-rhythms and phase relations in bodily contact reveal mechanisms of interpersonal resonance, contributing to understanding primary intersubjectivity, embodied affectivity, and affective intention with prototypes in early infant–caregiver interaction</cite>. In other words, the three dimensions do not just describe behavior; they specify the multimodal scaffolding by which protoconversational agents align agendas, map actions to meanings, and regulate each other’s states—operations that are the essence of intersubjectivity and fail if any dimension is absent or out-of-step.

Neurophenomenological support and the intersubjective channel

Trevarthen’s account has been linked to right-brain, multimodal systems for nonverbal social cognition, consistent with the view that coordinated kinematics–physiognomics–energetics ride on a dedicated intersubjective channel. <cite id="89102b51-2">Right temporoparietal junction and right-brain networks support face-to-face nonverbal communication; developmentally, right-brain intersubjectivity underpins mutual play and mutual love, with hyperscanning showing a co-constructed, nonverbal emotional communication system</cite>. Such neurocognitive architecture favors integrated prosody–gesture–face coordination over isolated channels; it explains why isolating one dimension (e.g., kinematic movement without facial/energetic modulation) yields at best mimicry, not shared meaning. <cite id="ad01463b-0">Prosody and gesture co-occur temporally and jointly influence semantic/pragmatic processing and emotion, suggesting that separating them degrades both informational and affective content</cite>.

Putting it together: why all three must operate together

- Mechanistically: kinematics supplies temporal phase-locking; physiognomics provides categorical mapping of state and action; energetics signals engagement and valence. <cite id="89102b51-1">Coordinating these three dimensions in imitation dynamically regulates the transfer of motives and emotions between minds</cite>. 
- Phenomenally: this multimodal alignment yields clarity of social intent, emotional nuance, and mutual coherence—hallmarks of intersubjectivity—rather than reflexive interaction. <cite id="ad01463b-1">Alignment across prosody, facial expressions, and gestures enhances communicative precision and recognition of mental states, supporting empathy and rapport</cite>. 
- Developmentally: these co-ordinated couplings scaffold protoconversations and attachment, with their absence or misalignment leaving only stimulus–response coupling. <cite id="35f15c40-2">Mutual coherence in emotional responsiveness builds attachment</cite>. 
- Neurocognitively: right-brain networks and hyperscanning evidence support a co-constructed, multimodal nonverbal system that integrates timing, form, and intensity. <cite id="89102b51-2">A right-brain-to-right-brain nonverbal emotional communication system underlies co-constructed relationships</cite>.

Therefore, Trevarthen’s framework requires all three dimensions to operate in coordinated synchrony because their integrated co-variation creates a multimodal coordinative structure—shared timing, category mapping, and energetic emphasis—that mutually regulates attention and intention, producing intersubjective understanding. When any dimension is missing or poorly coordinated, participants remain behaviorally interactive but lack the mutual coherence and shared meaning that define intersubjectivity. <cite id="89102b51-1">Coordinated kinematics, physiognomics, and energetics regulate transfer of motives and emotions and organize learning in communities</cite> <cite id="ad01463b-0">Prosody and gesture are tightly intertwined temporally and pragmatically, jointly conveying emphasis, emotion, and referential clarity</cite> <cite id="ad01463b-1">Fine-grained multimodal alignment enhances communicative precision and social intent understanding</cite> <cite id="35f15c40-2">Intersubjectivity emerges from mutual coherence in emotional responsiveness</cite> <cite id="89102b51-2">A co-constructed, nonverbal right-brain system supports this intersubjective coordination</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Psychology of the Embrace: How Body Rhythms Communicate the Need to Indulge or Separate
Snippet: The aim of the present study was to carry dynamic embodiment effects from body rhythms further into interactional resonance between persons, using observations of micro rhythms and their phases in an embrace; our study thus focused on the interactive aspects of kinesthetic/haptic body feedback effects. It may contribute to detect mechanisms of interpersonal resonance and further our understanding of communication of primary intersubjectivity (Trevarthen, 1979) [62], embodied affectivity (Fuchs & Koch, 2014) [32], and affective intentions (Shai & Belsky, 2011a; 2011b) [63,64], with prototypes stemming from early infant-caregiver interaction (Stern, 1985;Trevarthen & Delafield-Butt, 2013) [65,66]. The study further aims to synergize knowledge traditions from cognitive science (e.g., Gibbs, 2005) [16] and movement analysis (e.g., Kestenberg, 1995) [2] to contribute to a more informed embodied cognition and movement analysis research.

Title: The Interpersonal Neurobiology of Intersubjectivity
Snippet: I then cite recent brain laterality research on the essential functions of the right temporoparietal junction, a central node of the social brain, in face-to-face nonverbal communications. In the following section, I discuss the continued development of right brain intersubjectivity in the 2nd year and beyond, and the relational origins of the highly adaptive functions of mutual play and mutual love. In the final section, I offer thoughts on the clinical applications of Trevarthen's intersubjectivity and protoconversations in psychotherapy, offering very recent hyperscanning research that demonstrates a right brain-to-right brain nonverbal emotional communication system embedded in the co-constructed therapeutic relationship. I end by offering thoughts on the relationship between the affect communicating functions of the intersubjective motivational system and the affect regulating functions of the attachment motivational system.
